intuition: An undirected tree must connect every vertex and have exactly n - 1 edges. Check the edge count, then visit the graph from vertex 0. If all vertices are reached, those two facts together prove it is a tree; a disconnected graph cannot pass.

Build an undirected adjacency list by inserting both directions for each edge. Start at vertex zero and use a stack to visit all reachable vertices. Mark a neighbor when it is pushed, rather than when it is popped, so multiple adjacent vertices cannot schedule duplicate visits. The visited set also prevents repeatedly following the same undirected edge.

Why does this avoid a separate cycle detector? Every connected n-vertex graph contains a spanning tree using n-1 edges. If the graph itself has exactly n-1 edges, there are no extra edges left to form cycles. Thus the count check plus reaching all n vertices is both necessary and sufficient.
A singleton with no edges satisfies both conditions and correctly counts as a tree.

The explicit stack also handles a 2000-vertex chain within the stated domain. A recursive DFS would require one nested call per vertex and may exceed Python’s recursion limit; marking and pushing each vertex here keeps traversal depth in ordinary heap storage.

steps: For n=5 and edges [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[1,4]], there are four edges, matching n-1.
Build adjacency in both directions, then initialize visited={0} and stack=[0].
Pop 0 and mark/push neighbors 1, 2, 3. Four vertices are now known reachable.
Vertices 3 and 2 only lead back to already-visited 0.
Pop 1 and discover 4. Its only neighbor is the already-visited 1.
All five vertices were reached, so with four edges the graph is a tree; return true.

An undirected input edge must be traversable from either endpoint.
Mark on discovery so each vertex enters the stack once, even with several incoming visits.

keyDecision: Require both n - 1 edges and n reachable vertices.

concept.question: Why do connectivity and one-fewer edges certify an undirected tree?
intuition: Checking only reachability can accept a connected graph with cycles. Checking only the edge count can accept a disconnected graph whose cycle uses extra edges elsewhere.

An undirected tree with all vertices has exactly one fewer edge than vertices. Check that count, then traverse from one vertex and verify all are reachable. These two conditions together force the connected structure to have no cycle.
concept.observation: Require both full connectivity and exactly one fewer edge than vertices.
approach: Reject an edge count different from one fewer than the vertex count.
Traverse undirected neighbors from a starting vertex.
Accept only if all vertices were reached.
concept.correctness: A connected undirected graph needs at least one fewer edge than vertices to connect them all. If it had a cycle, one cycle edge could be removed while preserving connectivity, contradicting that minimum count. Therefore full connectivity with exactly that count implies an acyclic connected graph, precisely a tree.

complexity.explanation: Traversal examines vertices and undirected adjacency entries once. Work and storage are linear in vertices plus edges.

pitfalls: Require both full connectivity and exactly one fewer edge than vertices.
Do not reject the one-vertex zero-edge case.
